A classic example of a joke that is "so bad it's good" might be something like:

"Why don't skeletons fight each other? Because they don't have the guts."

At first glance, this joke might elicit an eye-roll rather than laughter. It's a pun—one of the most divisive forms of humor. The punchline hinges on a literal and figurative play on the word "guts": skeletons lack organs (literally no guts), and "having guts" also refers to courage. The joke is predictable, groan-worthy, and perhaps something you'd find in a Halloween-themed kids’ book. So why do some people find this kind of joke oddly delightful?

The Humor of Failure

The phenomenon of a joke being "so bad it's good" hinges on a kind of meta-humor: we’re not just laughing at the joke itself, but at its failure to be a "good" joke. This failure becomes a performance in itself. Here’s why this works:
